wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.mechanism: Drought attacks the restored peat asset through the water table. Across a rewetted Indonesian restoration area and its land-cover types, peat-surface subsidence accelerated sharply during and shortly after the 2019 El Niño drought when groundwater depths were very low, running at 2.5 to 4 times the rate of the preceding 3.5 years and more than double the 7.5-year mean (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_5). Rewetting does not remove the exposure: over the same long record a severe drought could still cause major water-table drops to near 1 m below the peat surface and associated carbon-emission spikes even in otherwise rewetted conditions, in restoration areas and in remaining peat swamp forest alike (ev_climate_shock_hooi24_6).
wetland_management__asset_threat__drough.conditionality: Both units come from a single Indonesian site in a single source, humid-tropical and upper-middle-income, so this is a sensitivity measured for tropical peat and nothing else — no temperate peat, no coastal or floodplain wetland type, and no second region is represented. The second unit is the authors' reading of their own record rather than an independent measurement. What the cell does establish is a project-design implication: a rewetting investment in drought-prone tropical peat should expect the asset to lose surface elevation and carbon in El Niño years regardless of how well the water management performs, and should budget and monitor for that rather than treat it as a failure of the works.

wetland_management__asset_threat__extrem.mechanism: The vulnerable asset is the canal dam that holds the water table up. In December 2005, after an extreme rainfall event, both dams in the Kalampangan Canal were damaged by water seeping underneath and along the sides; they were repaired in March 2006 and were damaged again in August 2006 (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_7). During an extreme rainfall event in August 2007 a further dam was damaged in a flash flood, the canal water level rising by several metres in a short period (ev_climate_shock_ritz13_8). The rainfall is the trigger; the vulnerability is structural, since highly permeable tropical peat lets seepage pass beneath and alongside a dam, and the sunken canals intercept overland and interflow, raising canal discharges when the rain is extreme.
wetland_management__asset_threat__extrem.conditionality: This is a single demonstration site in Indonesian tropical peat, recorded as a case study rather than measured across projects, and the repeat failure after repair is the most transferable part of it. It says nothing about damage to the wetland itself, about coastal or temperate wetland types, or about water-control structures of other designs. Read it as a design and maintenance risk for canal-blocking programmes in deep permeable peat — dam siting relative to the contour, seepage control, and a repair budget that assumes recurrence — rather than as a general sensitivity of wetland management to extreme rainfall. Provenance: humid-tropical, upper-middle-income, with no comparable record from any other peat region.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: Returning water is the lever: once hydrology and inundation are reinstated, habitat structure follows and mobile taxa arrive first. Vertebrate assemblages reached reference structure within a few years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_6), riverine and tidal wetlands recovered structure and function within a couple of decades (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_9), and most tidal-reinstatement monitoring studies documented biodiversity gains, including for commercially important fish (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3). Measured against a degraded baseline, restoration raised biodiversity overall and for vertebrates, vascular plants and terrestrial and aquatic invertebrates (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_3), and salt-marsh planting improved biodiversity against degraded wetland (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5). At landscape scale the gain is additive rather than per-site: each created wetland added species to the regional pool and the accumulation curve had not flattened, with benefit concentrated where the density of aquatic habitats rose substantially (ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1). Active intervention outperforms waiting: a planted basin stayed more diverse than its unplanted twin (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7), moss-layer transfer accelerated Sphagnum recovery towards intact cover (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3), enhanced practice reached intact-level specialist plant diversity within years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7), and active measures are what speed recolonisation of bare peat (ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10).
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Two different comparisons are mixed in this pool and they do not mean the same thing. Against a degraded or tidally restricted baseline the answer is a gain; against an intact reference wetland it is a shortfall. Biological structure and biogeochemical functioning of restored and created wetlands remained below reference sites a century after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_1), plant assemblage structure stayed below reference even then (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_7), restored peatlands carried markedly less Sphagnum and specialist cover than intact ones (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1), and inland depressional wetlands fed only by rainfall or groundwater had still not recovered to reference conditions decades after restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mm12_8). A second source disagrees outright - biodiversity in restored wetlands did not significantly differ from that in natural wetlands (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_2) - and that contradiction is itself the state of the evidence; it is kept, not averaged. How the work is done changes the answer as much as where: rewetting alone was projected to need several decades to reach intact cover (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4), passive restoration - simply stopping the damage - was projected over centuries (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5) with specialist cover stagnating or deteriorating long after abandonment (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6), and stressor removal without revegetation appeared to reduce specialist diversity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8). Measured harm is a minority but real: a small share of tidal-reinstatement studies reported negative outcomes, including a site whose most abundant fish was a non-native predator of the endangered species the project set out to protect (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2), while macrobenthos abundance and biomass (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7) and macroinvertebrate diversity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_meli14_4) did not respond at all. Nearly all of this is high-income temperate and boreal; the tropical signal is thin and bundled - spontaneous regrowth of native peat-swamp-forest trees was observed close to remaining forest and cannot be separated from the preceding clearing or from seed proximity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3) - and the Southeast Asian peat statement is a stated potential, not a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: On tropical peat, rewetting removes the drainage stress that keeps the site degraded, and where seed can still arrive the native community returns without planting: native peat-swamp-forest tree species were found growing spontaneously, at high density, in the most rewetted conditions of a restoration area (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to deliver enhanced biodiversity alongside litter supply to the upper peat, a stabilised microclimate and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Neither unit isolates the practice, so this row carries direction and nothing about size or speed. The Sumatran observation is explicitly a best case: every plot lay close to remaining forest, so seed arrival is easy, and the regrowth cannot be separated from the earlier clearing or from that seed proximity - no share of the outcome is attributed to rewetting alone (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). The companion statement is a potential the authors expect, not a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). Both come from upper-middle-income Southeast Asian peatlands, neither reports a comparison with an intact reference nor a time to recovery, and neither is from a low-income or farmed landscape - so for a humid-tropics scan this is a plausible-direction flag that needs local monitoring evidence before any magnitude is claimed, with distance to remaining forest the first thing to check on the ground.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In rainfed cropping landscapes the benefit comes from adding aquatic habitat where almost none remains. Catchment-scale wetland creation benefited the biodiversity of agricultural landscapes, particularly where the density of aquatic habitats rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each created wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness, with the accumulation curve still rising after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], and creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity in a landscape whose small waters had increased by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Establishment choices last: the planted basin remained more diverse in plant cover 10 years after planting than its unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7].
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Both studies sit in temperate, high-income rainfed cropland, Sweden and Ohio, and neither is a restoration of a lost wetland: they are wetlands created under a programme designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5] and a pair of pumped experimental basins [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. The 30% figure is a design condition on habitat density, not a measured effect size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The species gain is a regional accumulation across many wetlands, so it does not promise a gain at a single created site [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Ohio comparison is planting against natural colonisation within created wetlands rather than wetland against no wetland [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. Nothing here was measured in a tropical or low-income rainfed system, and no unit reports how the gain changes as the wetland ages.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: Restoring water and habitat structure brings species back, and in high-income temperate and boreal settings that is measured across several wetland types. Tidal reinstatement delivered biodiversity gains in most monitoring studies and positive effects on at least one commercially important fish species in most studies with species-level data (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3); salt-marsh planting improved biodiversity against degraded wetland (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5); each created wetland in a farmed catchment added species to the regional pool, with the landscape benefit arising once aquatic-habitat density rose substantially (ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1). Active intervention beats waiting: a planted basin remained more diverse than its unplanted twin (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7), moss-layer transfer brought Sphagnum cover towards and potentially past intact levels (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_3), enhanced practice reached intact-level specialist plant diversity within years (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_7), rewetting and tree felling produced marked recovery (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2), and active measures are what speed recolonisation of bare peat (ev_biodiversity_outcome_rasa23_10).
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Restored sites in this pool are better than degraded ones and still short of intact ones: Sphagnum cover and peatland specialist cover in restored peatlands were well below intact peatlands, across sites spanning a wide range of time since restoration (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_1). Which baseline is used therefore decides the sign, and the tidal review states its own positive bias - it counts an outcome as positive when it improves on the tidally restricted condition even where it never reaches a pristine reference (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1). Method decides the timescale: rewetting alone was projected to need several decades to reach intact cover (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_4), passive restoration was projected over centuries (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_5) with specialist cover stagnating or deteriorating long after abandonment (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_6), and stressor removal without revegetation appeared to reduce specialist diversity (ev_biodiversity_outcome_allan23_8) - so the budget line that pays for active revegetation is what separates a result in years from a result nobody alive will see. Harm and non-response are both present: a small share of tidal-reinstatement studies reported negative outcomes, including a non-native predator of the endangered fish a project aimed to support becoming the most abundant species (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2), and macrobenthos abundance and biomass did not respond to planting (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7). This row is in context for high-income settings only; it is the transfer source for poorer and warmer landscapes, not a statement about them.

wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.mechanism: In upper-middle-income tropical peatland, the operative step is rewetting: removing the drainage stress lets the native community re-establish where a seed source remains, with native peat-swamp-forest tree species growing spontaneously and at high density in the most rewetted conditions (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3). Restoring closed-canopy forest vegetation on degraded peat is expected to enhance biodiversity alongside litter supply, microclimate stabilisation and reduced fire risk (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4).
wetland_management__biodiversity_priorit.conditionality: Although this row is in context for its income band, the pool behind it is very thin and neither unit isolates the practice. The field observation is a stated best case - plots lay close to remaining forest, and the regrowth is bundled with the earlier clearing and with seed proximity, with no share attributed to rewetting itself (ev_biodiversity_outcome_hooi24_3); the companion claim is an expected benefit rather than a measurement (ev_biodiversity_outcome_mish21_4). Both are Indonesian and Malaysian peatlands, so the row speaks to tropical peat and not to other wetland types, to farmed landscapes, or to lower-income countries. No comparison with an intact reference and no recovery timescale is available here, so direction is all this supports; distance to intact forest is the first site-level check, and a monitoring commitment should accompany any investment scoped on it.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: The water table decides which gas the peat gives off, and that is why this row pools findings of opposite sign. Water-table decline stimulates heterotrophic rather than autotrophic soil respiration and raises the subsidence rate across climate zones and land uses [ev_wetflA_ma_wt_respiration], so drained peatlands release 645 Mt C yr-1 through soil respiration, about 5% of global annual anthropogenic carbon emissions [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release], with the highest per-hectare losses in the drained tropics [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates] and degraded peat already emitting 2 Gt CO2 a year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. Rewetting reverses the aerobic decomposition — reinstating the groundwater table substantially decreases carbon dioxide emission [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1] — but it also re-establishes methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2]. Both gases must therefore be named separately. Pooled across restored and altered wetlands, carbon dioxide flux fell significantly (SMD -0.43; CI -0.84 to -0.01; k = 111) while methane flux rose by an almost mirror-image amount (SMD 0.44; CI 0.14 to 0.74; k = 95) and nitrous oxide showed only a non-significant trend towards reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_3]; the carbon stocks moved unambiguously upward, soil carbon SMD 0.62, aboveground biomass 2.52 and belowground biomass 1.94 [ev_soil_organic_carbon_cama26_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_6], with the same pattern inside the peatland subgroup [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_7]. Where a source states a net balance over a stated horizon the balance is favourable: on a hundred-year global warming potential basis, rewetting drained organic soils gives net annual removals of carbon dioxide in most soil classes, an increase in annual methane, a decrease in nitrous oxide and dissolved organic carbon, and a lowering of net greenhouse-gas emissions [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_4]; every 10 cm the effective water-table depth is raised cuts the net warming of carbon dioxide plus methane together by at least 3 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 until the table is within 30 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1], and between 5 and 13 cm depth the carbon dioxide cooling exceeds the methane warming [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. Some sources refuse a fixed horizon and track radiative forcing through time instead, finding that it plateaus soon after rewetting because carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide stop while the re-established methane is short-lived, so the methane forcing does not undermine the mitigation and postponing rewetting raises long-term warming [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_5]. In the tropics the measured route is subsidence: canal blocking halved it where water tables rose from about -0.6 m to about -0.3 m [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_2], implying a carbon emission reduction of 6.4 to 23.6 Mg ha-1 yr-1 in the well-rewetted area [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi24_1].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: What the land was used for before rewetting decides the net result, and that is the finding rather than a caveat. On tropical cropland and plantation peat, rewetting caused an immediate, almost linearly increasing cooling, the rising methane offsetting only a few per cent of the cooling from falling carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3]. On temperate and boreal agricultural peat the warming from methane offsets a major part of that cooling for the first decades [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4]. On forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling for at least the first 40 years and still at least 50% a century later, and rewetting there also decreases the carbon stored in the trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_1]. Water held above the peat surface is the other sign flip: where average water levels are raised above the surface the warming from higher methane is likely to exceed the cooling from extra carbon dioxide sequestration over shorter horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; taking the table from 30 cm depth to the surface adds about 7 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], where stopping at 30 cm has a negligible effect, at most 0.3 [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3]. Hence the design rule of raising to 10-20 cm below the surface, which prevents a major portion of peat loss without causing high methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. Further reversals are kept rather than averaged away: higher emissions were estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]; an upland English rewetting raised methane significantly in the sparsely vegetated pans while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not move at all, so nothing on the carbon dioxide side offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up, ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]; cutaway-peat restoration cut soil carbon dioxide emission and raised methane, both driven by the same higher water table and vascular cover, and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]; a methane peak in the first years after rewetting has been reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6], consistent with carbon dioxide declining soon after restoration while methane rises in the short term [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_11, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_9]; and in seagrass the only significant restoration response was a rise in methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]. Much of the apparent disagreement in this pool is an artefact of the variable: there is no slot for an individual gas, so a carbon dioxide fall and a methane rise taken from the same sentence enter with opposite signs [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]. A second artefact is the comparator: the units recording restored wetlands falling short of intact reference wetlands — soil carbon still 50% lower after 20 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_2], organic matter at 62% of reference at 20-30 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_3], biogeochemical function at 79% of reference at 30 y in temperate and 53% at 50 y in cold climates [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_13, ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_12], peatland function still statistically lower 30 y on [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_11], and climate regulation the largest service shortfall [ev_carbon_sequestration_meli14_6] — say that restoration rebuilds a wetland slowly and incompletely, not that it loses carbon against the drained land it replaces. The tropical case is the weakest-supported and the most investable. The tropical rows of the water-table synthesis are extrapolated from temperate and boreal relationships rather than measured [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6], the tropical rewetting scenarios rest on default emission factors [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], and the source of those factors states plainly that no studies exist on rewetted tropical sites with the water table close to the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]. Measured tropical results are muted: a year after canal damming in Central Kalimantan, carbon dioxide emissions were 7305 then 7444 g m-2 yr-1 at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, read by the authors as no marked response [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site stayed a weak methane source and the source grew [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3] while the forest floor stayed a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4], and higher water tables had a relatively small effect on annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]. Raising the groundwater level hardly reduces peat-surface carbon dioxide flux in drained forest, because root respiration dominates it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]; regrowth on open restored areas is still too small to compensate peat decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3]; higher water tables did not completely compensate the increased subsidence near the canals [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5]; canal blocking is a long-term measure working through vegetation regeneration [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_1]; inside a drained plantation that stays in production the ceiling is a reduction of no more than 20% [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]; and the Southeast Asian reviews call the outcomes inconclusive, with decomposition continuing in the saturated zone and carbon leaving as methane or through fluvial networks, so a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural one [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_alex26_2]. Outside peat the gains are stock gains in temperate, high-income settings: soil organic carbon up 10.70 Mg C ha-1 against degraded wetland [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], organic matter in created-wetland surface soils up about 1% per 3-year period [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], nitrous oxide lower when plots were inundated [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9] but unchanged in upland plots the water never reached [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10], and methane up where flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8]. The general statements of potential carry no rate, country or climate zone [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3, ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_3, ev_carbon_sequestration_zou22_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_9, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_8].

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: In high-income temperate and boreal settings the mechanism is measured directly against the water table. Every 10 cm the effective water-table depth is raised cuts the net warming of carbon dioxide plus methane together by at least 3 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1, on a stated hundred-year global warming potential basis, until the table is within 30 cm of the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_1]; between 5 and 13 cm depth the cooling from carbon dioxide sequestration exceeds the warming from methane, giving a small net cooling on that horizon [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_5]. Halving drainage depths while the land stays in production cuts global carbon dioxide plus methane emissions by 65%, methane staying under 5 Mt CO2e yr-1 precisely because the table is not taken to the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7], worth 15.3 t CO2 ha-1 yr-1 on cropland organic soil [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_9]. On cutaway peat, restoration decreased soil carbon dioxide emission and raised net carbon dioxide uptake where the water table and vascular cover were higher [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1]; carbon dioxide losses fell after Canadian cutaway peat was restored and Finnish peatlands became a new sink within a few years [ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1]; a rewetted Irish site had a significantly reduced carbon dioxide emission factor of 104 g CO2-C m-2 yr-1, the sign indicating net uptake [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; and reed canary grass plots on cutover peat had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]. In coastal and created systems the stock terms move as well: planting raised soil organic carbon by 10.70 Mg C ha-1 against adjacent degraded wetland [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], organic matter in created-wetland surface soils rose by about 1% per 3-year period [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes were lower when marsh and edge plots were inundated [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Rewetting also reduces the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide emissions of peat drained for agriculture and forestry [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_2], and shallow lakes created on peat-extraction sites can reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: Prior land use decides the sign more sharply in this pool than anywhere. On temperate and boreal agricultural peat the warming from methane offsets a major part of the cooling for the first decades after rewetting [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_4]; on forestry-drained peat the increased methane offsets over 100% of the cooling from decreased carbon dioxide and nitrous oxide for at least the first 40 years, and still at least 50% a century later, while rewetting also decreases the carbon stored in the trees [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_5, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_1]. Taking the water table from 30 cm depth to the surface adds roughly 7 t CO2e ha-1 yr-1 of methane [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_2], where stopping at 30 cm has a negligible effect, at most 0.3 [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_3]; raising water above the peat surface is expected to warm over shorter horizons [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_4]; and moderate rewetting to 10-20 cm below the surface is the design that keeps both gases on the right side [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_6]. An upland English rewetting shows the trade-off unhedged: methane from the sparsely vegetated rewetted pans was significantly greater than from the vegetated haggs [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up], while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not change, so the carbon dioxide side did not offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]. Rewetting cutaway peat likewise increased methane as it cut carbon dioxide, both driven by the same higher water table and vascular cover [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2], and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance and higher sensitivity to climate anomalies than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]. In created riverine wetlands methane rose significantly once flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, though average emission from pulsed sites stayed below permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], the nitrous oxide benefit did not extend to upland plots [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions even while offering a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. Because there is no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide fall and the methane rise in these sources enter the pool with opposite signs; the sources themselves largely agree on the net direction. The scale figures are modelled rather than measured, and the tropical rows of that model are extrapolated from these temperate and boreal relationships, not observed [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_8]. Everything here sits outside the low- and lower-middle-income target: the measured sites are in the UK, Ireland, Canada, Finland, Estonia, the USA and China, and nothing in this scope row measures a tropical peat system.

wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.mechanism: This pool is not about gases at all. It holds the global loss-frame material and the comparisons of restored wetlands against intact reference wetlands, with no restored-against-degraded gas measurement in it. On the loss side, water-table decline stimulates heterotrophic rather than autotrophic soil respiration and raises the subsidence rate across climate zones and land uses [ev_wetflA_ma_wt_respiration]; drained peatlands release 645 Mt C yr-1 through soil respiration, about 5% of global annual anthropogenic carbon emissions [ev_wetflA_ma_global_release]; per-hectare heterotrophic respiration is highest in the drained tropics, at 10,865 to 23,685 kg C ha-1 yr-1 [ev_wetflA_ma_tropical_rates]; and degraded peat emits 2 Gt CO2 a year, nearly a quarter of land-sector emissions and up more than 25% since 1990 [ev_carbon_sequestration_bonn16_2]. That is the carbon restoration is meant to stop releasing. On the gain side, restored peatlands have lower carbon emission rates than degraded sites and over time can become net carbon sinks [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1], restoring degraded hydric soils has a high potential for sequestrating soil carbon [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2], and flooded wetlands provide the anoxic conditions optimal for accretion of organic matter [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3].
wetland_management__carbon_sequestration.conditionality: The negative sign in this scope row comes entirely from recovery-shortfall units measured against intact reference wetlands, not from any finding that restoration releases carbon relative to the drained land it replaces. Soil carbon in restored and created wetlands was still 50% lower than in reference wetlands after 20 y [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_2]; organic matter remained at 62% of the reference value 20-30 y after restoration [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_3]; biogeochemical function reached only 79% of reference 30 y on in temperate climates and 53% 50 y on in cold ones [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_13, ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_12]; peatland biogeochemical function remained statistically lower than reference 30 y after restoration even though biological structure recovered immediately [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_11]; and climate regulation was the largest of the individual service shortfalls against natural wetlands [ev_carbon_sequestration_meli14_6]. Read as their authors intended, these say that restoration rebuilds a wetland slowly and incompletely, so an intact peatland is worth protecting and a restored site should not be expected to match a natural one for decades. They do not say that a restored site sequesters less than the drained land it replaced, and no unit in this scope row makes that comparison. Both supporting gain statements are assertions of potential with no rate, country or climate zone attached [ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_2, ev_soil_organic_carbon_erwi09_3], and the general statement about restored peatlands becoming sinks is reported second-hand [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1]. Nothing in this row is a gas flux, a horizon-stated net balance, or a measurement in a low- or lower-middle-income setting.

wetland_management__coastal__asset_threa.mechanism: What wears a salt marsh away is the ordinary wave climate, not the cyclone. A global analysis of salt-marsh erosion and wave measurements found that most salt-marsh deterioration is caused by moderate storms of monthly frequency (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_6), while intense hurricanes contribute less than 1% to long-term salt-marsh erosion rates (ev_erosion_hazard_leon17_5) — the marsh survives the violent event and is eroded between them.
wetland_management__coastal__asset_threa.conditionality: Both units are drawn from the same sentence of the same review reporting the same global dataset, so this is a single line of evidence. It concerns lateral erosion of the marsh edge and no other failure mode, and it describes established marsh rather than a newly planted or recently restored one, where edge stability is likely to be weakest. The review's accompanying point is that retreat scales with wave energy rather than switching on above a critical storm, so the maintenance burden is continuous rather than event-driven: budget for steady edge retreat under the everyday wave climate rather than for post-cyclone repair. Provenance is high-income North Atlantic and European coasts.

wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.mechanism: Replanting marsh vegetation or reinstating tidal exchange rebuilds the habitat structure and the inundation regime that coastal species depend on. Against degraded or tidally restricted conditions this registers as a biodiversity gain in most monitoring studies and in the pooled planting analysis (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_5), with mobile and commercially relevant taxa responding most: birds were more abundant in planted marsh than in nearby natural marsh, and most studies with species-level data reported positive effects on at least one commercially important fish species (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_14, ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_3).
wetland_management__coastal__biodiversit.conditionality: The direction holds against a degraded or tidally restricted baseline and not against an intact one. Restored marshes carried significantly lower vegetation species richness than natural marshes, and lower macrobenthos richness with it (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_13), so the plant community that defines the habitat is the part that does not come back - while birds and fishery species do (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_14). A scoping read must keep those two comparisons apart rather than netting them. Non-response and harm are both recorded: macrobenthos abundance and biomass showed no major difference from degraded wetland (ev_biodiversity_outcome_liu24_7), and a small share of tidal-reinstatement studies reported negative outcomes, including a restored site whose most abundant fish was a non-native predator of the critically endangered native fish the project set out to support (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_2). Most units are shares of studies or effect sizes rather than measured magnitudes, which is why the class is held at moderate, and the tidal review states that counting an outcome positive whenever it improves on the restricted condition may overstate positive results (ev_biodiversity_outcome_tidal26_1). The evidence is high-income coastal, dominated by the United States, with planting dominated by a single genus.

wetland_management__coastal__carbon_sequ.mechanism: Coastal restoration works through carbon stocks rather than through the peat gas balance. Planting salt marsh increased soil carbon storage against degraded wetlands (effect size 0.21), alongside gains in shoreline protection, primary productivity, biodiversity and fishery production [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4], and raised soil organic carbon stocks by 10.70 +/- 3.45 Mg C per hectare relative to adjacent degraded wetlands, with aboveground and belowground biomass up 237.88 and 479.18 g per square metre [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. Measured against a natural marsh rather than a degraded baseline, restored marshes matched the reference on carbon dioxide flux (Hedges' g* = 0.03, n = 86, not significant) and on soil organic carbon accumulation rate (64.26 against 64.72 g per square metre per year, n = 18), and emitted significantly less methane (g* = -0.21, n = 70) [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11, ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. In saline systems sulphate suppresses methanogenesis, so the methane penalty that dominates freshwater rewetting is largely absent here.
wetland_management__coastal__carbon_sequ.conditionality: The negative direction of this row rests on a single subgroup result in a single preprint: among wetland types, seagrass showed only a significant increase in methane flux, with no offsetting significant benefit [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_10]. That result is real and is not hidden, but it carries the row against the salt-marsh findings because it is weighted as a meta-analysis, while its own authors note that seagrass beds were under-represented in the dataset and that tropical and southern regions are a major geographical gap. Seagrass and salt marsh are not interchangeable, and the only methane result in salt marsh points the other way [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_12]. Comparator matters too: the gains are measured against degraded wetland, which is the counterfactual a restoration project faces [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_4, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6], while the equivalence results are measured against natural marsh and say that restored marshes accumulate carbon as fast as natural ones even while their stocks lag [ev_soil_organic_carbon_liu24_10, ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_11]. The salt-marsh evidence is high-income and overwhelmingly North American, European and East Asian, with planting dominated by a single genus, and some plantings also received fertiliser or protective structures [ev_carbon_sequestration_liu24_6]. Nothing in this row is a tropical mangrove or a low- or lower-middle-income coastal system, and no unit states a net balance over a stated horizon.

wetland_management__coastal__cost_per_he.mechanism: Every unit in this row comes from the same global salt-marsh review, which reports project budgets divided by the area restored. Mean total cost per hectare at unprotected sites is USD 495,067-876,564 in middle-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_1] and USD 454,285-694,724 in high-income countries [ev_project_cost_wang22_2]. Broken out by method, within the middle-income unprotected cell, hydrological restoration costs USD 6,090-9,945 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_3] while vegetation restoration costs USD 26,945-42,756 [ev_project_cost_wang22_4]. What a coastal project does therefore drives its cost far more than where it is done.
wetland_management__coastal__cost_per_he.conditionality: A single source carries the whole row, so there is no cross-source check on it. The headline per-hectare totals are flagged by the compilers as implausibly high for a landscape intervention: project areas are small and the budgets include engineering, hard structures and land, so the ordinal reading (coastal restoration is expensive, and hydrological work is its cheapest component) is what transfers, not the number. The quoted ranges are the spread across the review's alternative monetary conversion methods, not confidence intervals. The evidence base is China, Great Britain, the Netherlands and the United States; it is not a low- or lower-middle-income cost, and tidal and marsh engineering costs should not be carried to inland or smallholder settings.

wetland_management__coastal__cost_reduct.mechanism: Both units come from the same global tidal-reinstatement review and both describe cost rising, not falling. Tidal reinstatement is often more cost-intensive than other types of coastal wetland restoration because it requires hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility assessments, spatial modelling and complex regulatory compliance and permits [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5]. Reported project costs vary widely with scale and setting: Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta at 128,000 ha cost US$20.1 million, against US$1.17 million for the 38 ha Galilee Saltmarsh Restoration in the United States [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4].
wetland_management__coastal__cost_reduct.conditionality: A single source carries the row, and it reports project totals with no comparable per-hectare denominator, so the two schemes cannot be put on the same scale without arithmetic the source does not perform. Nothing here measures avoided or reduced cost, so the target name overstates what the pool contains. The reviewed projects are concentrated in the United States, Australia and England, with Colombia the sole upper-middle-income case, and the review's own emphasis is that government funding is what carries the upfront cost — a condition that cannot be assumed in a low- or lower-middle-income investment.

wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.mechanism: Salt marsh dissipates wave energy and takes height off a surge as it travels across the platform. Wave heights fall by 72% across salt marsh, with a 95% confidence interval of 62 to 79% in a meta-analysis of field measurements (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1); up to 82% of wave energy is dissipated over marsh against 29% over the adjacent sand flat (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_3); storm-surge attenuation rates run from 1.7 to 25 cm per kilometre of marsh depending on marsh and storm characteristics (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_1). The vegetated-versus-unvegetated contrast is consistent — salt marsh vegetation had a significant positive effect on wave attenuation, and every paired study comparing vegetated marsh with intertidal mudflat concluded attenuation is greater over the marsh (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_1, ev_flood_hazard_shep11_2).
wetland_management__coastal__flood__all.conditionality: What has been measured is wave attenuation under ordinary conditions: the meta-analysed measurements are all taken under normal conditions of low waves (ev_flood_hazard_nara16_1). The function weakens exactly where protection is wanted — attenuation works less effectively during extreme storms lasting more than a day, which the review reads as a reason not to rely on nature-based flood defences alone in populated low-lying coastal and estuarine areas (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_2). Floodwater attenuation inside the marsh, meaning flood-peak reduction and floodwater storage, has never been quantified: the systematic review found no study evaluating it (ev_flood_hazard_shep11_5). Siting can cancel the benefit, since levees and dikes behind a marsh cause water to set up against the structure and limit the surge-attenuating effect (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_4). The remaining support is self-reported: 41% of salt-marsh projects state that such habitats provide improved protection from storm events (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). Provenance: existing marsh rather than restored marsh, on high-income US, UK, Dutch, Belgian, Italian and Vietnamese coasts, with coastal property and society as the beneficiary rather than the farm.

The function weakens where protection is wanted — attenuation works less effectively during extreme storms lasting more than a day, which the review reads as a reason not to rely on nature-based flood defences alone in populated low-lying coastal and estuarine areas (ev_flood_hazard_leon17_2). The remaining support is self-reported: 41% of salt-marsh projects state that such habitats provide improved protection from storm events (ev_avoided_damage_value_nara16_4). Provenance: existing marsh rather than restored marsh, on high-income US, UK, Dutch, Belgian, Italian and Vietnamese coasts, with coastal property and society as the beneficiary rather than the farm.

wetland_management__coastal__rural_pover.mechanism: The entire row is coastal protection economics. Salt-marsh nature-based defences carry a replacement cost ratio against a submerged breakwater averaging 2 (0.95-3.01) [ev_economic_return_nara16_3], with marsh projects running from just as expensive to around three times cheaper than the engineered alternative depending on water depth [ev_economic_return_nara16_6], although the same review states the defences are not always cost effective [ev_economic_return_nara16_5]. About 40% of salt-marsh restoration projects recover their investment cost within 30 years [ev_economic_return_wang22_5], and adding carbon sequestration value shortens the recovery period at both the low and the high carbon price tested [ev_economic_return_wang22_6].
wetland_management__coastal__rural_pover.conditionality: This row does not measure poverty, income or any household outcome; the beneficiary in every unit is society, and the benefits are avoided storm damage, avoided engineering cost and, in part, modelled carbon value. The cost recovery share excludes maintenance and running costs and rests on benefit data covering only a couple of ecosystem services, both of which push the share up; the replacement cost ratio spans the no-difference value and is recorded as not significant. The evidence is from China, Great Britain, the Netherlands, the United States and Vietnam, almost entirely high-income, while the target is low- and lower-middle-income. Read the class as a statement that coastal wetland projects can compete with hard engineering on cost where protected assets are valuable, and not as a statement that they lift rural households out of poverty.

wetland_management__coastal__soil_erosio.mechanism: Marsh vegetation attenuates waves and currents as water passes through the canopy, so suspended sediment settles, the bed accretes and surface elevation is maintained while lateral erosion of the shoreline is reduced. That mechanism is measured from both ends: inside existing marsh against adjacent unvegetated mudflat, where most paired studies reported increased accretion or surface elevation or reduced erosion and the pooled effect on shoreline stabilisation was positive (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4); and in planted marsh, which improved shoreline protection against degraded wetland (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3) and trapped sediment at least as well as the adjacent natural marsh (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15).
wetland_management__coastal__soil_erosio.conditionality: Much of the pool is not a restoration result at all: the paired-study evidence measures what EXISTING marsh does against bare mudflat (ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_3, ev_erosion_hazard_shep11_4), which is an argument for protecting marsh that is already there rather than a measured gain from creating or replanting it, and a sizeable minority of those paired studies did not report a positive effect. The planted-versus-natural trapping estimate is hedged by its own authors (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15), and the restored-versus-degraded pooled values are effect sizes and shares of studies whose scale the sources do not define (ev_erosion_hazard_liu24_3), which is why direction is firmer than magnitude here. This is shoreline and tidal-flat erosion only - it carries nothing about soil loss from cropland or rangeland - and the field sites are high-income coasts in the United States, United Kingdom, China and the Netherlands, with the authors noting that matched restored and degraded pairs are few.

wetland_management__coastal__water_quali.mechanism: A planted salt-marsh canopy slows tidal flow and waves, so suspended particles and the nutrients and contaminants bound to them drop out of the water column and are trapped in the marsh instead of moving on. The measured expression of that here is sediment trapping by planted marsh, which matched or bettered the adjacent natural marsh (ev_sediment_retention_liu24_15).
wetland_management__coastal__water_quali.conditionality: The row rests on a single meta-analytic estimate that its own authors hedge, and the comparison is against adjacent NATURAL marsh - so it says a planted marsh traps sediment at least as well as an intact one, not what the gain is over an unvegetated shore or over doing nothing. Sediment trapping is also a proxy for particulate and turbidity load, not a measurement of nutrient or contaminant removal; nothing in this pool measures nitrogen or phosphorus. The underlying studies are concentrated in North America, Europe and East Asia and are high-income coastal settings, with no observation from a low- or lower-middle-income farmed catchment, and the practice is marsh planting dominated by a single genus - a different intervention from the inland nutrient-retention wetlands that carry the main water-quality case.

wetland_management__coastal__wind_cyclon.mechanism: Coastal wetland standing between a cyclone and exposed property reduces the damage done, measured as an elasticity across US Atlantic and Gulf coastal counties: a 1% loss of coastal wetlands is associated with a 0.6% increase in property damage (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_1). Valued at the margin, the median county's wetland is worth about $91,000 per km2 per year in storm protection, against an average of about $1.8 million and a range from less than $800 to $100 million per km2 (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_4), and a counterfactual on a single hurricane put the damage attributable to prior wetland loss at about $430 million (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_5).
wetland_management__coastal__wind_cyclon.conditionality: Protection is proportionately smallest where the storm is strongest: the elasticity of property damage with respect to wetlands is 0.58 for a tropical storm and 0.35 for a category 3 to 5 hurricane (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_2, ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_3). Built defences substitute for it — the elasticity is 0.50 in states with stricter building codes against 0.81 where codes and enforcement are weaker (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_6). All of this is measured on existing wetland cover rather than on a restoration project, and the same authors warn that a replacement wetland may take decades to fully develop the functions of the wetland it replaces (ev_avoided_damage_value_sun20_7), so the measured value is not what a new project delivers. Provenance: a single US panel study of high-income coastal counties; the outcome is damage to coastal property, a societal and asset-owner benefit rather than a rural livelihood one, and nothing in the cell speaks to a low-income or lower-middle-income coast.

wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Per-hectare cost in this pool is an artefact of what each source counted, not a price for a technology. Gourevitch et al. feed US agency unit costs into a floodplain model at USD 3,200 per hectare for wetland revegetation and USD 6,400 per hectare for forest revegetation — labour and materials only, with the land easement priced separately and excluded [ev_project_cost_gour20_5]. Wang et al. instead divide whole salt-marsh project budgets by the area restored, which puts unprotected sites in middle-income countries at USD 495,067-876,564 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_1] and unprotected sites in high-income countries at USD 454,285-694,724 [ev_project_cost_wang22_2]; within that same table the method of restoration separates the costs far more than the income band does, with hydrological restoration at USD 6,090-9,945 per hectare [ev_project_cost_wang22_3] against USD 26,945-42,756 for vegetation restoration [ev_project_cost_wang22_4]. Alexandra et al. report a secondary Indonesian national average of about USD 1,866 per hectare, drawn from a national restoration total of USD 1.7 to 7 billion [ev_project_cost_alex26_1].
wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: These figures must not be averaged, converted or annualised against each other. Each rests on a different denominator: a modelled unit cost that excludes land; total project cost divided by restored area, which the compilers themselves flag as implausibly high for a landscape intervention because project areas are small and the budgets carry engineering and land acquisition; and a national average cited from other work, with no currency year, no breakdown between rewetting, revegetation and revitalisation, and no statement of the area the national total is divided by. The evidence comes from China, Great Britain, Indonesia, the Netherlands and the United States, so nothing here prices a rural restoration in a low- or lower-middle-income landscape, and the engine emits no value range at this scope. The usable reading is ordinal and within-source: hydrological works are the cheap end of a wetland budget and planting, engineering and land acquisition are the expensive end.

wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.mechanism: Both units describe high-income coastal and floodplain work. Gourevitch et al. use agency unit costs of USD 3,200 per hectare for wetland revegetation and USD 6,400 per hectare for forest revegetation, covering labour and materials and excluding the land easement, which that paper prices separately [ev_project_cost_gour20_5]. Wang et al. report mean total cost over restored area for unprotected high-income salt-marsh sites at USD 454,285-694,724 per hectare, the cell holding 62.4% of the reviewed studies and therefore the modal case of the global salt-marsh record [ev_project_cost_wang22_2].
wetland_management__cost_per_hectare_res.conditionality: The emitted span from USD 3,200 to USD 694,724 per hectare is the distance between two incompatible accounting conventions — a modelled input cost for planting versus a whole project budget divided by the area restored, including engineering and land — and is not an uncertainty interval around a central value. Neither figure states a currency year in the quoted passage. This row is scoped to high-income contexts and cannot set a value for a low- or lower-middle-income investment; it is usable only as an upper bound on what engineered coastal restoration has cost where land and labour are expensive.

wetland_management__cost_reduction.mechanism: Nothing in this pool measures a cost being reduced; the units describe where wetland work is costly and why. The global tidal-reinstatement review states that, compared with other types of coastal wetland restoration, tidal reinstatement is often more cost-intensive, because it requires hydrological engineering, land acquisition, feasibility assessment, spatial modelling and regulatory compliance [ev_project_cost_tidal26_5], and that project costs vary widely — Colombia's Ciénaga Grande de Santa Marta at 128,000 ha cost US$20.1 million, while the smaller Galilee Saltmarsh Restoration in the United States at 38 ha cost US$1.17 million [ev_project_cost_tidal26_4]. On the peatland side, the paludiculture scoping review attributes weak farm economics partly to high investment costs of wet cultivation, including the need for specialised harvesting equipment and adapted production processes, and to higher risk than conventional drainage-based peatland use [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3].
wetland_management__cost_reduction.conditionality: The target name is cost reduction, but every unit in the row is a cost-increase statement; no class is emitted for a cost row, so nothing is being asserted, and a reader scanning the target alone would be misled. The project totals cannot be turned into per-hectare costs: the source gives budgets and areas for deliberately contrasting schemes, and dividing them out is the extractor's arithmetic, not a claim of the source. The evidence sits in Australia, Colombia, Germany, Great Britain, Indonesia, Latvia, the Netherlands and the United States, overwhelmingly high-income; any cost saving in a low- or lower-middle-income setting would have to be established locally.

wetland_management__creation__biodiversi.mechanism: Creating wetlands in farmland adds habitat that the landscape has lost, and the new basins can reach the standard of the old ones. Dual-purpose created wetlands sustained alpha, beta and gamma diversity similar to that of natural lentic water bodies in the region [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2], and the pollution-sensitive stoneflies, mayflies and caddisflies made up almost twice as large a share of richness in the created wetlands, 19%, as in the reference ponds, 10% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. Catchment-scale creation benefited landscape biodiversity, particularly where aquatic habitat density rose by at least 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]; each new wetland added between 1.44 and 32.67 species, median 2.70, to regional richness with no asymptote after 36 wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3], so creating more wetlands continuously enhanced regional diversity where small waters had risen by 20 to 30% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_5]. Planting at creation left a lasting mark: the planted basin was still more diverse in plant cover 10 years on than the unplanted control [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7].
wetland_management__creation__biodiversi.conditionality: Most of these findings state a direction without an effect size, which is why the class does not run higher. Two of the strongest results are comparisons against mature natural ponds rather than against a no-wetland baseline, so they say the created wetlands are as good as the existing ones, not how much the landscape gained by building them [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_4]. The evidence is temperate and high-income throughout, Sweden and Ohio, and the Swedish wetlands were designed and sited mainly for nutrient retention [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_1]. The species gain is regional and cumulative, not a promise for a single basin [ev_biodiversity_outcome_thie09_3]. The Ohio contrast is planting against natural colonisation inside created wetlands [ev_biodiversity_outcome_mits05_7]. No tropical or lower-income measurement is present, and no unit reports whether the invertebrate advantage holds as the wetlands age and fill with sediment.

wetland_management__creation__carbon_seq.mechanism: Creating a wetland builds a new carbon store from scratch. In created riverine basins in Ohio, organic matter in surface soils increased by approximately 1% per 3-year period over the decade after construction [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6], and nitrous oxide fluxes from marsh and edge plots were lower when those plots were inundated than when the same plots were exposed to air [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_9]. Shallow lakes created on former peat-extraction sites had the potential to reduce net greenhouse-gas flux through carbon sequestration [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].
wetland_management__creation__carbon_seq.conditionality: The methane cost of putting water onto land sits in the same sources. Methane emission from vegetated areas rose significantly when flooding reached zones that previously had no standing water, although average emission from pulsed sites stayed below that of permanently flooded sites [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_8], and the created shallow lakes caused methane emissions to the atmosphere even as they offered a net flux reduction [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_9]. The nitrous oxide benefit reaches only as far as the water does: in the upland plots, fluxes did not differ between flooded and dry periods [ev_carbon_sequestration_mits05_10]. Because the register has no variable for an individual gas, the carbon dioxide and nitrous-oxide gains and the methane rise from the same experiment enter the pool with opposite signs, which makes the evidence look more divided than it is: both sources report a net gain with a methane penalty inside it. The row rests on a pair of pumped experimental basins in temperate Ohio and a review of boreal and northern European peat-extraction after-use. No unit states a net balance over any horizon, none measures how the balance changes as the created wetland matures, and none is from a low- or lower-middle-income setting [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mits05_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_8].

wetland_management__creation__flood__all.mechanism: Created storage intercepts part of the storm volume before it reaches the receptor: the review reports that reduction of peak discharge by online and offline storage areas is effective and notable in both fieldwork and modelling results (ev_wetflA_zhu_storage_effective), online storage being blocking within the drainage network and offline storage being retention and detention features set aside from the channel.

The remaining reversals are kept rather than averaged away: higher emissions were estimated from rewetted temperate nutrient-rich forest sites than from their drained counterparts [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_5]; a rewetted Irish peatland emitted more methane than natural sites and its global warming potential was still above intact peatland after a decade, even though its carbon dioxide emission factor had fallen significantly to 104 g CO2-C m-2 yr-1 [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_7]; a fertilised reed-canary-grass plot on cutover peat emitted 21,938 kg CO2 ha-1 yr-1 against 8,448 from the natural bog, although the same plots emitted far less methane than the bog and had lower global warming potential than bare peat [ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_6, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_5]; an upland English rewetting raised methane significantly in the sparsely vegetated pans while photosynthesis and ecosystem respiration did not move, so nothing on the carbon dioxide side offset it [ev_wetflA_gatis_methane_up, ev_wetflA_gatis_co2_null]; cutaway-peat restoration cut soil carbon dioxide emission and raised methane together, and after a decade some restored sites still showed a more warming balance and higher sensitivity to climate anomalies than intact peatland [ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_rasa23_3]; a methane peak in the first years after rewetting has been reported [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_6]; and the peatland subgroup records methane rising significantly alongside its carbon dioxide and stock benefits [ev_carbon_sequestration_cama26_8]. Much of the apparent disagreement here is an artefact of the variable rather than of the literature: there is no slot for an individual gas, so a carbon dioxide fall and a methane rise taken from the same sentence enter with opposite signs [ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_gunt20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_tan21_2]; and the one recovery-shortfall unit says peatland biogeochemical function remained statistically lower than reference wetlands 30 y after restoration, which is a statement about rebuilding an intact peatland, not about losing carbon against the drained baseline [ev_soil_organic_carbon_mm12_11]. The tropical evidence is the thinnest and the most investable. The tropical rewetting scenarios rest on default emission factors [ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_3], and the source of those factors states plainly that no studies exist on rewetted tropical sites with the water table close to the surface [ev_carbon_sequestration_wils16_1]; the tropical rows of the water-table synthesis are extrapolated from temperate and boreal relationships rather than measured [ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_6]. Measured tropical results are muted: a year after canal damming in Central Kalimantan, carbon dioxide emissions were 7305 then 7444 g m-2 yr-1 at the forest site and 2781 then 2608 at the deforested burned site, read by the authors as no marked response [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_2]; the deforested site stayed a weak methane source and the source grew [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_3] while the forest floor stayed a weak sink [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_4]; higher water tables had a relatively small effect on annual methane budgets [ev_carbon_sequestration_jauh08_5]; raising the groundwater level hardly reduces peat-surface carbon dioxide flux in drained forest, because root respiration dominates it [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_2]; regrowth on open restored areas is still too small to compensate peat decomposition [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_3]; the higher water tables did not completely compensate the increased subsidence near the canals [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_5]; canal blocking is a long-term measure that works through vegetation regeneration rather than on its own [ev_carbon_sequestration_ritz13_6]; inside a drained plantation that stays in production the ceiling is a reduction of no more than 20% [ev_carbon_sequestration_hooi12_1]; and the Southeast Asian reviews call the outcomes inconclusive, with decomposition continuing in the saturated zone and carbon leaving as methane or through fluvial networks, so a rewetted peatland cannot be expected to behave like a natural one in its gas exchange [ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_mish21_2]. The remaining tropical claim is a direction-only review line about a bundled rewetting and fire-prevention programme, with no magnitude and no comparator [ev_carbon_sequestration_alex26_2], beside general statements of potential [ev_wet_carbon_sequestration_ramsar18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_erwi09_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_ojan20_8, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_7, ev_carbon_sequestration_evan21_9].

wetland_management__peatland__cost_reduc.mechanism: A single statement carries this row: the paludiculture scoping review attributes the weak farm-level economics of wet peatland cultivation to higher risks than conventional drainage-based peatland use, to high investment costs — including the need for specialised harvesting equipment — and to production processes that have to be adapted [ev_wet_cost_neud26_3]. The direction is an increase in cost relative to the drained baseline, carried here as the inverse of a cost reduction.
wetland_management__peatland__cost_reduc.conditionality: The unit is a narrative statement cited from other work, with no magnitude, no currency and no denominator, so it can support a direction and nothing more. Its evidence base is predominantly high-income European peatland, with the remainder largely Indonesian, and the comparator is a drained agricultural system that is already generating income — which is the relevant baseline in Germany, Latvia or the Netherlands but not necessarily in a low- or lower-middle-income landscape. Nothing in the row establishes any cost saving from peatland management; it says the opposite, that wet use costs the operator more than the drained use it replaces.

wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.mechanism: Re-vegetating bare peat and blocking grips and gullies raises surface roughness and storage on the hillslope, so storm water is delivered more slowly. Peak discharge fell 27% at a re-vegetated micro-catchment and 51% where gully blocking was added, both against a bare control (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_O, ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_N), and 49% at a rewetted peat gully (ev_wetflA_gatis_peakflow); lag between peak rainfall and peak flow lengthened significantly at the re-vegetated site (ev_wetflA_shut_lag_O), restoration elsewhere produced lower discharge rates observable at drain and hill-stream level, with greater water-table stability and a reduction in peak flows (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_field), and modelling suggests drain blocking in blanket peat could reduce flood flows downstream (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_model). The loss frame points the same way: higher flood peaks and shorter times to peak go with peatland degradation and removal of vegetation cover (ev_wetflA_dads_degradation_loss, ev_wetflA_acre_barepeat_loss). Peak and timing do not behave alike as storms grow — at the gully-blocked site the peak reduction held at 56% in the largest storms while the lag gain collapsed (ev_wetflA_shut_peakq_largestorm_N, ev_wetflA_shut_lag_largestorm_N) — and at the rewetted gully the lag shortened even as the peak fell (ev_wetflA_gatis_lag_reversal). Restoration changed the timing and the peak of delivery but not the volume: the runoff coefficient was unchanged at both restored sites (ev_wetflA_shut_runoffcoef_null).
wetland_management__peatland__flood__all.conditionality: The measurements are plot to micro-catchment; the catchment-scale benefit is not demonstrated. No effect was found at the scale of the entire 260 km2 catchment (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_catchment_null), the influence of drain blocking on flood flows has been notoriously difficult to detect at basin scale (ev_wetflA_acre_drainblock_basin_null), the monitoring authors state that isolating restoration effects within empirical storm-flow datasets is problematic at the large catchment scale (ev_wetflA_shut_catchment_undetectable), and a realistic suite of land-management changes modelled against an extreme rainfall event gave a median flood-peak reduction of only 2% (ev_wetflA_dads_scamp_model_2pct). Position decides the sign: upland wetlands tend to be flood-generating areas, frequently saturated with little water storage potential (ev_wetflA_acre_position_upland); blanket bogs close to saturation for most of the year rarely attenuate flow and are much more likely to contribute to storm runoff (ev_wetflA_acre_saturated_bog_reversal); a moorland scheme designed to delay runoff synchronised sub-catchment peaks and increased downstream flood risk (ev_wetflA_shut_synchrony_reversal); and an on-site storage gain can still raise peaks at catchment scale (ev_wetflA_acre_synchrony_catchment). Even on the hillslope the lever is conditional: ditch blocking in upland peat reduces flow peaks only in the steepest, smoothest drains, with the roughness of the surrounding vegetated peat mattering more than the ditches (ev_wetflA_dads_ditchblock_conditional), and upland ditches may increase or decrease local flood peaks depending on layout, topography and synchronisation (ev_wetflA_dads_ditch_sign_flip). The review covering this family reports moderate flood-reduction results but without empirical evidence for larger-scale effects (ev_wetflA_zhu_peatland_confidence). Provenance: UK blanket peat carries almost the whole cell, with a Chinese high-altitude degradation case and a Newfoundland bog; it is temperate and high-income, with no low-income or lower-middle-income measurement, and the benefit arrives downstream rather than on the plot.
